Let \(y_i=\cos x_i\). Then \(y_i\in[-1,1]\), \(\sum y_i=0\), and
\[
\cos(3x_i)=4\cos^3x_i-3\cos x_i=4y_i^3-3y_i.
\]
Thus
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{10}\cos(3x_i)
=4\sum_{i=1}^{10}y_i^3-3\sum_{i=1}^{10}y_i
=4\sum_{i=1}^{10}y_i^3.
\]
So we maximize \(\sum y_i^3\) subject to \(y_i\in[-1,1]\) and \(\sum y_i=0\).

Let the positive \(y_i\)'s sum to \(P\), and suppose there are \(m\) negative \(y_i\)'s. For fixed \(P\), the maximum positive contribution is obtained by taking as many positive entries as possible equal to \(1\), while the negative contribution is maximized by spreading the negative magnitudes equally, giving
\[
\sum y_i^3 \le P-\frac{P^3}{m^2}.
\]
The optimal \(P\) is an integer; then \(m\le 10-P\), and this expression increases with \(m\), so \(m=10-P\). Hence
\[
\sum y_i^3 \le P-\frac{P^3}{(10-P)^2},
\]
where \(0\le P\le 5\). Checking:
\[
\begin{aligned}
P=1&:\;1-\frac1{81}=\frac{80}{81},\\
P=2&:\;2-\frac18=\frac{15}{8},\\
P=3&:\;3-\frac{27}{49}=\frac{120}{49},\\
P=4&:\;4-\frac{16}{9}=\frac{20}{9},\\
P=5&:\;5-5=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
The maximum is \(\frac{120}{49}\), attained by taking three \(y_i=1\) and seven \(y_i=-\frac37\). Therefore
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{10}\cos(3x_i)\le 4\cdot \frac{120}{49}=\frac{480}{49}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\frac{480}{49}}
\]
